Breckland's population increased by around 11,000 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 140,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Breckland increased by 8.4%, from just under 130,500 in 2011 to around 141,500 in 2021.

The population here increased at a similar rate to the overall population of the East of England (8.3%), but by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Breckland was home to around 0.8 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 0.7 in 2011. This area was the joint least densely populated local authority area across the East of England.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was similar in Breckland to the East of England as a whole

An older Breckland

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Breckland increased by two years, from 44 to 46 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the East of England as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 4,000 (an increase of 15.3%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just over 2,000 (7.8% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.3 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Unpaid care in Breckland

In 2021, 4.3% of Breckland residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 6.8% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 50 people (1.9%) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.4% in 2011. The proportion of Breckland residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care remained at 2.8%.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Breckland (2.5 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East of England (2.8 percentage points, from 7.3% to 4.5%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Breckland decreased by 2.5 percentage points

Religion in Breckland

In 2021, 42.1% of Breckland residents reported having "No religion", up from 27.6% in 2011. The rise of 14.6 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Breckland. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the East of England, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.9% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 50.0% of people in Breckland described themselves as Christian (down from 63.8%), while 6.3% did not state their religion (down from 7.4% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 42.1% of usual residents in Breckland reported having "No religion"

Breckland residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 123,100 Breckland residents said they were born in England. This represented 87.0% of the local population. The figure has risen from just under 116,100 in 2011, which at the time represented 89.0% of Breckland's population.

Poland was the next most represented, with around 2,900 Breckland residents reporting this country of birth (2.0%). This figure was up from around 2,100 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.6% of the population of Breckland.

The number of Breckland residents born in Portugal rose from around 1,500 in 2011 (1.1% of the local population) to around 1,800 in 2021 (1.3%).

In 2021, 87.0% of Breckland residents reported their country of birth as England

National identity in Breckland

In 2021, 7.7% of Breckland residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 6.5% in 2011.

In 2021, 1.1% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.4% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Breckland that identified as "British only" increased from 12.4% to 51.4%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the East of England (2.1 percentage points, from 6.9% to 9.0%) than in Breckland (1.2 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Breckland increased by 1.2 percentage points

Family in Breckland

Of Breckland households, 20.1% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 21.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in six households (17.4%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 19.5% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children increased from 6.1% to 6.5%.

This area had the region’s third highest percentage of households including a couple but no children. Across the region, only Mid Suffolk (21.5%) and South Norfolk (20.5%) had a higher percentage of households including a couple but no children.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Breckland decreased by 1.7 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Breckland residents aged 16 years and over, 30.4% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 26.6% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in two people (49.4%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 52.9% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Breckland that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.9% to 10.7%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership in Breckland (3.9 percentage points) was similar to the increase across the East of England (3.7 percentage points, from 31.1% to 34.8%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Breckland increased by 3.9 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Breckland residents aged 16 years and over, 54.6% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 55.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 1 in 50 people (2.1%) said they were unemployed, compared with 3.1% in 2011. The percentage of retired Breckland residents increased from 27.3% to 28.5%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed in Breckland (1.3 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East of England (1.1 percentage points, from 58.4% to 57.3%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Breckland decreased by 1.3 percentage points

Change in work hours

In 2021, 10.8% of Breckland residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 10.2% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in eight people (13.3%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 15.7% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 54.9% to 56.2%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week in Breckland (0.7 percentage points) was similar to the increase across the East of England (0.4 percentage points, from 10.4% to 10.8%). Across England, the percentage increased by 0.6 percentage points, from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Breckland increased by 0.7 percentage points

Change in housing in Breckland

Of Breckland households, 67.0% owned their home in 2021, down from 68.6% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in six households (18.1%) rented privately, compared with 15.2% in 2011. The percentage of Breckland households that lived in a socially rented property increased from 13.8% to 14.1%.

The decrease in the percentage of households that owned their home was greater across the East of England (2.4 percentage points, from 67.6% to 65.2%) than in Breckland (1.6 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.0 percentage points, from 63.3% to 61.3%.

The rate of home ownership in Breckland decreased by 1.6 percentage points

Disability in Breckland

In 2021, 7.3% of Breckland residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 8.3% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Breckland (1.0 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East of England (1.2 percentage points, from 7.8% to 6.6%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Breckland decreased by 1.0 percentage points

Health in Breckland

In 2021, 44.7% of Breckland residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 43.1% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 37.4% to 36.8%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Breckland residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.0% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" was 3.9% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Breckland increased by 1.6 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Breckland

In 2021, 0.6% of Breckland residents identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group"), up from 0.1% in 2011. The 0.4 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the East of England, the percentage of people from the "Other ethnic groups" ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.5% to 1.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 1.0% to 2.2%.

In 2021, 96.5% of people in Breckland identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.4% in 2011), while 1.4% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.2% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category increased from 0.8% in 2011 to 0.9% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
